newsitem.title: UK: Flemings backs Latam despite uneasy Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: Flemings backs Latam despite uneasy Wall Street.

text.p: Robert Fleming & Co said on Tuesday Latin America remained its top emerging market regional pick despite difficult developed market conditions.
In its monthly emerging markets focus, Flemings said that of the three IFCI regions of Latin America, Asia, and Europe Middle East and Africa (EMEA), it remained overweight in Latin America.
The report said Asian and Latin American markets had tended to be highly sensitive to Wall Street in the past, but had fallen by less than expected following recent U.S. losses.
"Assuming the restoration of a degree of equilibrium in developed markets, we fell that Latin America will once again be the focus of global investor liquidity," it said.
"With a continuing good supply of company stories, we see widespread potential for gains - with Brazil remaining our favourite large market."

Flemings Latin American regional analyst Walter Stoeppelwerth said the increased participation of local investors in Argentina, Brazil and Peru and the economic recovery cycle in all the major countries were behind the maturity of Latin American markets in the face of global volatility.
"We still favour Brazil and Colombia for superior valuations. Argentina, Mexico, Peru and Venezuela are neutral bets on recovery while Chile lacks a trigger," he said.
Flemings also said it had raised its holdings within EMEA in smaller sub-Saharan African markets and South Africa.
In addition to positive economic and political fundamentals and generally attractive valuations, the markets all have low or negative betas versus the FT World Index, it said.
It recommended investors have 13 percent of an EMEA portfolio in sub-Saharan Africa and 50 percent in South Africa, up from five percent and 38 percent respectively in March.
Exposure to Russia and Egypt was reduced to accommodate the shift, but the two remained Flemings' largest IFCI non-index bets.
Many Asian markets tumbled in the wake of the U.S. interest rate rise and international capital flows into the markets remained small, it said.
But it said that Asia could ride out the upswing in U.S. rates with much less damage than in 1994/95.
"We highlight Malaysia, India and Hong Kong as continuing to offer value. Structural problems are deepening in Thailand and Korea."
